newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain indicates troubles ahead for EU treaty.
newsitem.headline: Britain indicates troubles ahead for EU treaty.

text.p: Britain told its European Union partners on Friday what they already knew -- that negotiations over the next six months on a new EU treaty will be an exercise in frustration.

At a summit of leaders from the 15-nation bloc, British Prime Minister John Major reeled off a list of policies that London would not sign up to, effectively gutting the main thrust of 11 months worth of negotiating.

By contrast, French President Jacques Chirac said a document prepared by the Irish EU presidency outlining the direction of treaty negotiations was a "useful contribution" but did not go nearly far enough to be considered a draft treaty.
"We need substantial reform," Chirac told his colleagues.

The blueprint for the new treaty, drawn up by the current Irish EU presidency, shows the Union heading towards closer cooperation in crime fighting, joint employment policies, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
It also calls for the EU to create by 2001 a single Europe embracing freedom, security and justice and ensuring the free movement of people.

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said the leaders had welcomed the report and that it was clearly the basis for negotiations between now and the planned signing of a new treaty at a summit in Amsterdam in June 1997.
But he also admitted that a mighty effort would be needed.
"(Agreeing the new treaty will) need the sort of inspiration which was had by those who framed the original constitution of the United States of America in the 1780s," he said.
Major, however, made it clear that Britain was ready to wield its national veto against anything that smacks of a loss of national sovereignty.

He warned that the concept of "flexibility" in which some countries integrate ahead of others had to be handled carefully. "The wrong sort of flexibility...would blow the European Union wide apart," he told reporters.
France and German have called for a flexibility clause in the treaty that would allow countries to move ahead, using EU institutions, without the unanimous approval of all members.
Major also scoffed at plans for an employment chapter in the treaty that would make job creation a formal goal of the Union. "Declarations of that sort will not create a single job," he said.
He also reiterated that Britain would not give up its veto in any area and was firmly opposed to any role by the European Commission or European Parliament in justice or home affairs.

Most of Britain's EU partners have accepted that little if any progress towards a new treaty is likely to come before the next British election, to be held by May next year and which Major is expected to lose.
Privately, many expect the end of the treaty negotiations will have to be extended beyond the Amsterdam summit in order to allow a new British government to find its feet.
Chirac, who with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has called for far deeper EU integration, said more EU cooperation was needed in justice and home affairs and foreign policy.
Effectively rebutting Major, he said that if the EU was to expand as planned to as many as 20 members, it was necessary to change the way EU institutions work radically.
